items.excerpt: #### Police detain protesters during march to ECI HQ A march against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was halted by police in central Delhi on Friday (October 23, 2026), as participants sought to head towards the Election Commission of India (ECI) headquarters to protest against the alleged deletion of voters. items.title: Early Edition: October 23, 2026
items.excerpt: RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR ... Russian President Vladimir Putin yesterday said that future talks on a settlement of the war in Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both countries and an overall framework for security throughout Europe. Putin said the peace should be in its “final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time.” Vladimir Soldatkin reports for Reuters. Trump on Wednesday called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine, U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal. The sources said the system was working more normally yesterday shortly after their conversation. Trump told Musk he was frustrated the system’s speeds remained capped. Trump yesterday said Musk had restored Ukraine’s Starlink access but declined to comment when asked about if he had spoken to Musk about the matter. Alexander Ward and Lara Seligman report; Jacob Bogage and Kanishka Singh report for Reuters. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov today told reporters that reports that U.S. citizen Stephen James Hubbard was released in exchange for the recent release of Russian war blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk from custody in Montenegro were false. Dmitry Antonov reports for Reuters. A tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel is heading towards New York, ship-tracking data viewed by Reuters showed today. The tanker is the first to be transferred to the United States after Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel. ISRAEL-HAMAS WAR Israeli strikes and gunfire in Gaza yesterday killed at least four people, according to local health officials. In Gaza City, a strike on a car killed at least one person, another strike killed a Palestinian man on a bike in the southern city of Khan Younis, and a strike killed a man near Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza. Gunfire killed a woman near the northern Jabalia refugee camp. The Israeli military said it had struck Hamas militants in Gaza City, Khan Younis, and Nuseirat, but that it was not aware of the reported incident in Jabalia. Nidal al-Mughrabi reports for Reuters. WEST BANK DEVELOPMENTS The Israeli military today said they prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron when they shot and killed two men. The IDF said the two men were carrying guns. The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later instructed security forces to cordon off Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank. Shlomo Mor and Sam Mednick report for AP News. ... A pair of studies published today in the Nature Health journal say severe heat killed more than 50,000 people in European cities and towns this summer. Researchers said that the figure is three times as many people as would have died had manmade global warming not occurred. The studies are based on a combination of factors that influence heat-related health risks in particular locations, and the estimates are not based on official death reports. Raymond Zhang reports for the New York Times. The International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Ecosystems yesterday announced that almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs have now been classified as critically endangered. It was the group’s first global assessment of shallow-water reef ecosystems, and it said heat stress because of climate change is the overwhelming reason for the finding. Catrin Einhorn reports for the New York Times. OTHER GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS

items.title: US business activity cools in October; strong demand fueling price pressures By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US business activity slowed modestly in October, though robust demand allowed companies to raise prices for goods and services, a sign that inflation could increase further and remain persistently high in the coming months. S&P Global said on Friday its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, which tracks the manufacturing and services sectors, slipped to 57.6 this month from a five-year high reading of 58.4 in September. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. Strength in manufacturing was offset by a slight pullback in the vast services sector. The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing following what is expected to have been a strong performance in the July-September quarter. Economists expect the government’s advance gross domestic product report next week to show the economy growing at around a 3.0% annualized rate last quarter, mainly driven by consumer spending and business investment in AI. The economy has so far not shown any signs of buckling under the weight of the oil price shock stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran, with savings, generous tax returns in the spring, tariff refunds, a strong stock market performance and corporate profits providing a cushion. Economists warned that the inflation fallout from the drawn-out Middle East conflict was likely to slow consumer spending this quarter. The survey’s measure of new orders received by businesses edged up to 58.2 this month, the highest level since March 2022, from 58.1 in September. The increase was mostly in the services sector, with S&P Global noting "rising domestic demand, boosted partly by precautionary stock building" and growth in exports. ... Its gauge of prices for output rose to 59.8, the highest reading since August 2022, from 58.4 in September. Businesses across manufacturing and services sectors raised prices. Delivery performance by suppliers to manufacturers deteriorated further. The survey’s measure of suppliers’ delivery times dropped to a more than four-year low of 38.1 from 40.9 in September. SUPPLY BOTTLENECKS INTENSIFYING ... "Cost pressures remain a key concern," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers." ... Consumer and producer prices increased strongly in September, the government reported this month, raising concerns that inflation was fanning out across the economy. The Federal Reserve in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range. ... items.title: Live updates: Donald Trump tries to tackle gas prices, heads to Florida for rally
items.excerpt: President Trump will rally voters closer to home Friday afternoon, with a campaign stop in Fort Myers, Fla., as long-awaited midterm elections approach. He’ll be there to boost Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who’s running for governor, and Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), who is running for a full Senate term. Trump invoked the Defense Production Act on Thursday, announcing the government would spend $150 million toward boosting domestic gas and diesel production as the White House looks to ease consumer pain at the gas pump. He touted the move Thursday night in Iowa. The president also leaned further into the controversy surrounding Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s advertisement. The ad, which emerged late Monday, features Democrat Amy Acton’s mother claiming she is a “liar.” It has drawn fierce opposition from Democrats and some Republicans. But Trump and Vice President Vance are among those defending the video. ... ## Cook Political Report shifts 19 House seats in Democrats' favor Nonpartisan election forecaster Cook Political Report has shifted 19 House seats in Democrats’ direction less than two weeks before the midterm elections, according to its latest report published Friday. The shift includes six seats held by Republicans that were previously noted as a “Toss Up” and have now been changed to “Lean Democrat”: Reps. Juan Ciscomani (Ariz.), Gabe Evans (Colo.), Jen Kiggans (Va.) and Derrick Van Orden (Wis.). ... “Following this latest round of ratings changes, Democrats now are favored outright in the 218 seats they need to win control of the House,” Cook Political Report’s U.S. House of Representatives editor Erin Covey wrote in the report. “Republicans, meanwhile, are favored in 198 seats, rated Solid, Likely, or Lean Republican. That leaves 17 races rated as pure Toss Ups.”

items.title: Up First briefing: War on Iran; Midterm early voting; Trump vs. BBC : NPR
items.excerpt: Heavier fighting in Iran could resume in the coming weeks as military reinforcements arrive and some U.S. personnel leave the region. This shift comes as a person briefed on the U.S. and Israel's war planning told NPR that the countries were preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran after the U.S. midterms. Iran said it is prepared. Traffic in ... - 🎧 There are clear signs of preparations for a possible attack, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. The U.S. is deploying a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently visited Israel to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. President Trump will likely consider military action after Nov. 3 to avoid a spike in oil prices before the midterm elections. In response, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Iran is ready for both diplomacy and war. While the U.S. and Israel possess the power to inflict heavy damage, Iran shows no signs of making significant concessions, Myre says. Instead, it demands formal control over the Strait of Hormuz and the withdrawal of U.S. troops from the region. Although Election Day is more than a week away, almost 21 million Americans have already voted, either by mail or early in-person voting, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab. - 🎧 That number of votes so far is a lot and is an increase of about 2 million since yesterday, according to NPR's Saige Miller. In key battleground states, early voting is significantly higher compared to the last midterm election. While the early voting data should not be overinterpreted as a predictor of final results, it shows Democrats voting at higher rates than Republicans, Miller says. Unaffiliated voters are also participating early. Democrats are generally more likely to vote early, and Republicans are more likely to turn out on Election Day, Miller says. - ➡️ A federal judge in California is limiting the Department of Homeland Security's pre-election field operations. The agency says they aim to identify noncitizens who allegedly voted illegally in nine states. - ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab. ... Trump must sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation case against the BBC, a federal magistrate judge ruled. Trump is required to comply with court rules or face sanctions, the judge said yesterday. The case centers on a Panorama broadcast from late October 2024, which allegedly edited the president's Jan. 6 speech to make it appear he incited a violent siege of Congress. Trump has described the broadcast as false, misleading and defamatory under Florida law. - 🎧 It's unclear if Trump will sit for a deposition after he previously canceled for "matters of national importance" and suggested January as an alternative, NPR's David Folkenflik says. The case initially focused on the economic harm the broadcast posed to Trump's brand and financial prospects. Although the BBC apologized for the splicing, it now seeks to understand Trump's mindset during his testimony, as he may have intended to encourage violence. BBC attorneys say more than 200 defendants from Jan. 6 said Trump's speech motivated them. The BBC is actively pursuing details about how Trump has profited since regaining the White House, most likely to assess the extent of the damage he faces, Folkenflik says.

items.excerpt: Why big music stars like Harry Styles and Celine Dion are embracing residencies ... NEW YORK (AP) — Harry Styles' residency at Madison Square Garden has drawn tens of thousands of fans eager for an exclusive experience. His run is the latest in a trend. Residencies are growing among pop stars, with artists like Bad Bunny, Usher and Carín León embracing the style of performance. Residency pioneer Celine Dion has also returned to the format. Industry insiders say residencies offer benefits like reduced travel stress and elaborate stage productions. However, some fans argue that costs are shifted to them, with high ticket prices and travel expenses to see the shows. While residencies provide artists a break from touring, experts emphasize the importance of traditional tours to reach fans who can't travel. NEW YORK (AP) — An Emmy-winning actor known for roles in “Top Gun” and “Picket Fences,” Tom Skerritt has died at 93. His family said in a statement he died Wednesday of natural causes. Skerritt won an Emmy for “Picket Fences” in 1993 and was known for roles in “Turning Point,” “Steel Magnolias,” and “Contact.” He was once described as a character actor in a leading man’s body. Skerritt also performed onstage, including in “Our Town” and “A Time to Kill.” His family highlighted his passion for storytelling and helping others. ... The beloved children's musician Raffi continues to charm audiences with his timeless songs. Fifty years after his debut children's album, his music remains a staple for young children. Raffi's latest album, “Love is Everywhere,” comes out Friday. It features songs celebrating everything from individuality to the importance of voting. He believes that while technology changes, the essence of childhood remains the same. In an interview with The Associated Press, Raffi emphasized the importance of protecting children's development from excessive technology. He also discussed his commitment to not exploiting children through advertising and how it caused him to turn down a movie offer for “Baby Beluga.” NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Country Music Hall of Famer John Anderson has died at age 71. His family announced his death Wednesday on his social media accounts. Anderson was known for his high, yearning vocal style and hits such as “Swingin’,” “Wild and Blue,” and “Black Sheep.” Born in Apopka, Florida, he moved to Nashville, Tennessee, after high school. He worked odd jobs before his commercial breakthrough in 1977. Anderson was a “New Traditionalist,” sometimes compared to George Jones and Merle Haggard. He was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024 and won two Country Music Association awards. LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jay-Z once called John Legend “our voice,” but Pharrell Williams had a different idea for Legend's baritone. On his new album, “Muse,” Legend dials back his powerhouse vocals, opting for a more conversational delivery at Williams’ urging. The album, out Friday, marks Legend’s first full collaboration with Williams after more than 20 years of friendship. Recorded mostly at Williams’ studio in Paris, it grew from Legend’s appearance on Clipse’s “The Birds Don’t Sing.” In an interview, Legend discussed Williams’ influence, Jay-Z’s compliment and composing his first original stage score for a new musical.
